Bachet's Magic Trick

CountingLogicInvariants
Game: Pick a pair of numbers from a list, then watch the computer guess your pair from just two row choices.
How to play: Click a pair and press Proceed. Find your two numbers in the grid, click the row each one is in, and see what the computer says.

Stage 1 · the list of pairs

How many numbers 4
Look for the math

A spectator thinks of a pair of numbers, and the computer names it after being told only which two rows hold them. Nothing is memorised: the whole trick is the way the cards are laid out.

Counting the pairs

With N numbers, the pairs you can make (letting a number pair with itself) number N(N+1)/2. For N = 4 that is ten pairs, from {1,1} through {4,4}. Each number turns up in exactly N + 1 of those pairs, counting a doubled pair like {1,1} twice. The logic test checks both counts for every N from 3 to 6.

The hidden pattern

The applet actually prints N(N+1) cards — two for every pair — in a grid with N rows and N + 1 columns. The two cards of the pair {a, b} are put in rows a and b (twice in the same row when a = b). With N = 4 and a straight, unshuffled list the grid is:

1 2 3 5 7
4 9 10 11 13
6 12 15 16 17
8 14 18 19 20

Notice that the doubled pair {a, a} sits in columns a and a + 1: its companion is exactly one column to the right of its row number. The logic test reproduces this whole table from the applet's own layout rules.

Why two rows are enough

Because of that layout, the two rows a pair occupies identify the pair and no other pair shares them. Naming the rows a and b therefore recovers the two card numbers. Permuting the cards within rows, or swapping which of the two a pair's cards goes to which row, never changes the rows involved. The test checks this for every pair, at every size, with Straight and Randomize both on and off — the computer always names the right pair.

Turn on Straight list and turn off Randomize to see the pattern clearly, then switch Randomize back on and watch the trick still work.
